newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. shut out of U.N. money panel, France, N.Z. in.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shut out of U.N. money panel, France, N.Z. in.

text.p: In a surprise move, the United States has been ousted from a key United Nations finance committee, mainly because of its $1.4 billion debt to the world body, United States officials and diplomats said.

Instead, France and New Zealand on Friday were given seats on the prestigious 16-member Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions (ACABQ), which plays an important role in reviewing the U.N.'s $1.3 billion annual budget.
It was the first time the United States, the largest single contributor assessed for 25 percent of the U.N. budget, did not get a place on the panel of financial experts.

Many diplomats thought the United States would regain its seat next year and the close vote was a momentary pique at American attempts to drastically cut U.N. costs while it failed to pay its own contributions.

But U.S. envoys immediately told their colleagues they would have more trouble than ever now getting funds from the Republican-dominated U.S. Congress, which has been extremely critical of all activities by the United Nations.

France received 117 votes followed by New Zealand with 116 and the United States with 103. French envoys said they did not campaign against Washington, assuming it would get one of the two vacant seats for which it was eligible automatically.
The other 14 members of the group of financial experts are from Russia, Cuba, Barbardos, Brazil, China, Germany, India, Italy, Japan, Mali, Romania, Syria, Tanzania and Tunisia.
Asked why the United States lost, an American official said: "Three things: money, money and money. The resentment of U.S. arrears to the United Nations was clearly the decisive factor.
"The lack of our participation will inevitably diminish the committee," she added.

The vote by secret ballot was in the General Assembly's administrative and budgetary committee, which includes all 185 countries with U.N. membership. It makes the final decision on the budget, which the Assembly then usually rubber stamps.

U.S. officials pointed out that American envoys would still play a major role in the main budgetary committee. But they admitted it was a blow not to be involved in the initial fine print of the budget.

Western diplomats said the U.S. debt was the main factor. Another, they said, was the un the U.S. delegate who had served on the panel for years. She was to be replaced by Melinda Kimble, who diplomats said was not yet well known and was facing two strong candidates, Gerard Biraud of France and Denise Almao of New Zealand.
The ACABQ examines U.N. regular and peacekeeping budgets as well as those of specialised agencies.
The United States owes the world body about $1.4 billion for past dues and current and past peacekeeping costs -- more than half of the U.N.'s entire debt.
